The Natural History of the Sea-Serpent

Published in Koot-Hoomi’s Quarterly, New Lovegain, 1341.

The patron who does us the honor to take up this article, as a gentle preparative for an after-dinner nap, may, perhaps, pardon us for reminding them that the soft turquoise light of their sitting-room lamp is borrowed from the largest and most ferocious of known creatures; that the oil which turns night into day, and invests its power upon the steam-engines of our manufactories and rail-roads, once formed part of a vast and fearsome being whose heart sent out twenty or thirty gallons of blood at every stroke, through an aorta measuring more than two feet in diameter; and that the creature whose gigantic frame was nourished by this flood of life gamboled on the broad back of the World-Ocean, rejoicing in its strength, till the minuscule, mortal human, whose engines had grown hungry for the wyrms’ treacly ichor, made war upon the beast in its own realm, and left the enormous mass inanimate. Nor is every one acquainted with the dangers and privations borne by those who seek the terrible monster in its remote watery demesne. A serpent-hunting voyage often exceeds three years, and hardly ever occupies less than two. From the port of New Lovegain alone an average of seventy sail of fine ships, of a burthen ranging from three to four hundred tons, are annually on the look-out for the fattest of sea-serpents. The crews of these ships, which are fully provisioned for three years, and sail from New Lovegain at all times of the year, consist of from twenty-eight to thirty-three sailors and officers—including at least one sorcerer, typically a tempestarius also serving as navigational astrologer, which, after all, seems to us to be a very commendable species of mixed practice. As, for obvious reasons, there are in such expeditions “no more cats than can catch mice,” the mariner who has been afloat in one of these ships is pretty sure to turn out a crack specimen of their genus—a smart character, case-hardened to any climate, expert in all their professional duties—endued with imperturbable nerves and quick decision, eagle-eyed, and tyger-hearted.

All the sailors are, in point of fact, co-adventurers with the owner; for they go “on the lay”—that is, they have a certain share of the produce, instead of the ordinary money-payment. This arrangement, which sailors find eminently favorable to employment in the smoky labyrinths of New Lovegain’s rail-fed manufactories, can be ascribed to the influence of the Mazuraa cultus, particularly those clades which favor the worship of the Deep Goddess in Her incarnation as Gykylyk, Mother of Storms. Such teachings have long argued that the great serpents, being ex nihilo and tempore ruinae the creation of their favored goddess, therefore exist as the common property of humankind, who have worked for over a millennium to appease the deities’ displeasure. The rewards of the serpents’ oil, the sea-laborers have proclaimed, should then at least be shared equitably amongst the crew who procured the stuff.

The zeal with which this dangerous sea-hunt is pursued seems to take the strongest possession of the sailors’ minds; and one of their most usual modes of making a heavy hour light is sketching their favorite ship, serpents in various attitudes, and the hair-breadth escapes of their companions and themselves, upon the tooth or bone of one of the monsters whom they have seen die. One of the grandest examples of such craft I have seen was upon a ship that patrolled the waters between the southern New Lands and San Borondon, executed upon a yard-long tooth. Its panoramic image was of the fearsome creature from which it was plucked, pictured “in a flurry” and pursued by a spate of skiffs from a finely-detailed schooner, but pierced with almost as many darts as the fabled Archemedon Wyrm slain by the sea-monks of San Borondon in Ontic antiquity. Though the creature’s vast powers must have been well-known long before the scriptural age, the natural history of the sea serpent has, since antiquity, been the opprobrium of zoologists and magi alike. It would be wearisome to detail all the distressing confessions of almost every philosopher who has approached this fell class of animals, even though perfectly aware of the difficulties of this subject. One of the most common debates within scientific circles turns around the question of whether the various sea serpents found around the World-Ocean, which range in size, coloration, fang dentation, etc., may constitute a single breed of creature, or a collection of separate species. The result of this experience is to confirm the opinion hazarded by Professor Zarxas, that there is but one known species of sea serpent. He says:—”It is not my intention, were it in my power, to enter into the inquiry as to the true method of dividing the hydracea into groups, families, genera, or species; but this I can assert in contradiction to Doctor Oucoumiche, and other authorities, that there is no more than one species of sea serpent, and this I say from having particularly noticed their external form, and also their manner and habits, in various parts of the world very distant from each other. The large full-grown male appears the same in every part, from New Lovegain to the Cassiterides, from the Cassiterides to the tip of Norumbega, from Norumbega to San Borondon; while their females coincide in every particular, having their young ones among them in the same order, and appearing similar to all others which I had seen in every respect, merely differing a little in color, length or fatness, according to the climate in which they were captured.”…

How to Love the World More: Artist and Poet Rachel Hébert’s Breathtaking Catalogue of Gratitudes

Here we are, living these lives bright and perishable as a poppy, hard and shimmering as obsidian. We know that they are entirely improbable, that we bless that bright improbability with each flash of gratitude for it all, that if we pay attention closely and generously enough we are always repaid in gladness, that it is the handle of the door to the world. And yet over and over we choose to live in the cage of complaint, too preoccupied with how the will of life betrayed our wishes, the wanting monster always growling in the other corner of the cage.

Imagine parting the bars and stepping out. Imagine waking up with a rush of gladness at everything we were never promised but got anyway — trees and music, clouds and consciousness, the cobalt eye of the scallop, the golden fan of the gingko, the alabaster chandelier of the ghost pipe.

In our age of competitive prostration, this is a headstand hard to hold for long. But it is trainable. It is possible to become strong enough to be tender, it is.

Artist and poet Rachel Hébert offers a bright patch of training ground in The Book of Thanks: A Catalogue of Gratitudes — one of the most miraculous books I have ever encountered, trembling with tenacious tenderness for the bewilderment of being alive.

Radiating from the pages is an invitation, extended in paintings and poems, to open “the sunlit fort of your attention” and let the world rush in, in all its minute and majestic loveliness: stalactites and Spanish moss, spiderwebs and skylights, snow and the call of the snowy owl, the heart’s capacity for “an urgent, flashing, interrupting kind of love.”

What emerges is prayerful (“more cellos, touch, and rain, please”) and singing with praise (“roots gripping, canyon carved, spine woven of baleen a thousand years old”) — a manual for how to live in gratitude (“what is working wants your praise”) and a theological statement (“there is nothing you must do to belong”).

A taste:

What do we say to longing?

If you have sat in the chill

of early morning bleakness

and watched as the deep blue

sighed and blushed, touched

by the warm curve of dawn

and pinker than pink then

apricot soft and spreading its

glow, you know. You know.

How

— in this dim parade of brutality —

might all be well?

But if we trouble it with light,

train our sights on

the rebellious good,

and work

to make it

truer.

Beneath the face

of the water,

wonder.

In dark woods,

a gate.

In the chapter

called lostness,

a friend.

All the help

we could not

yet see.

It cannot be always comfortable.

So love the thousand knives as they enter

and see your shape still sitting.

See that you too belong to paws

of soft silent hungers, to thirst-tangled

roots, to silver-spun constellations.

Know you’re no sicker than the rest of us.

The big secret is this: No one else can brave you.

Messy, yes. And marvelous.

What is more than we see

in this world we’re pressed into,

its blistered barking noise?

For what we build, speak, and ruin —

our efforts, our angers.

For music.

For wings.

—

Published November 25, 2026

item.title: The Paradox of “Finding Yourself”
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

The Paradox of “Finding Yourself”

“No one can build you the bridge on which you, and only you, must cross the river of life,” thirty-year-old Nietzsche wrote in his treatise on how to find yourself. And yet in the century and a half since, a curious dissonance has begun to reverberate across culture: On the one hand, we have grown increasingly fixated on the self as the focal lens for interpreting the world — a fixation which Ian McEwan so brilliantly satirized and which has precipitated today’s tragic epidemic of militant identity politics; on the other hand, the rise of neuroscience has demonstrated again and again that the self we experience as so overwhelmingly real — the psychophysiological raft of experience through which we float along the river of life — is a sensory-perceptual byproduct of consciousness, completely illusory in its solidity.

Nearly half a century ago, the Pulitzer-winning poet Robert Penn Warren (April 24, 1905–September 15, 1989) cast a cautionary eye to the notion of “finding oneself” in Democracy and Poetry (public library) — his magnificent Jefferson Lecture about power, tenderness, and art’s role in a healthy society.

Decades before Harvard psychologist Daniel Gilbert’s witty and wise observation that “human beings are works in progress that mistakenly think they’re finished,” Warren challenges the cultural trend of young people taking “time off” from school or work in order to “get away from it all” and find themselves. He writes:

In the phrase [“to find myself”] lurks the idea that the self is a pre-existing entity, a self like a Platonic idea existing in a mystic realm beyond time and change. No, rather an object like a nugget of gold in the placer pan, the Easter egg under the bush at an Easter-egg hunt, a four-leaf clover to promise miraculous luck. Here is the essence of passivity, one’s quintessential luck. And the essence of absurdity, too, for the self is never to be found, but must be created, not the happy accident of passivity, but the product of a thousand actions, large and small, conscious or unconscious, performed not “away from it all,” but in the face of “it all,” for better or for worse, in work and leisure rather than in free time.

In consonance with my own deep belief in the ongoingness and fluidity of our becoming, Warren adds:

The self is a style of being, continually expanding in a vital process of definition, affirmation, revision, and growth, a process that is the image, we may say, of the life process of a healthy society itself.

In a sentiment that calls to mind Academy of American Poets executive director Jennifer Benka’s beautiful observation that “poems are physical sites of discovery [and] sense-records of our humanity,” Warren considers the role of poetry as a locus of our evolving being:

How does poetry come into all this? By being an antidote, a sovereign antidote, for passivity. For the basic fact about poetry is that it demands participation, from the secret physical echo in muscle and nerve that identifies us with the medium, to the imaginative enactment that stirs the deepest recesses where life-will and values reside. Beyond that, it nourishes our life-will in the process of testing our values. And this is not to be taken as implying a utilitarian aesthetic. It is, rather, one way of describing our pleasure in poetry as an adventure in the celebration of life.

Complement this particular portion of Warren’s thoroughly transcendent Democracy and Poetry with Walt Whitman on identity and the paradox of the self and philosopher Rebecca Goldstein on what makes you and your childhood self the “same” person despite a lifetime of change, then revisit Elizabeth Alexander on what poetry does for the human spirit.

—

Published November 25, 2026

Teens from across the U.S. perform as the Macy’s Great American Marching Band

Macy's is celebrating the 100th edition of its famous Thanksgiving Day Parade. We meet the students from around the country who join together to play in its signature marching band.

SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade will not be on Thanksgiving Day this year. It has been moved to Saturday due to what are expected to be major storms in and around New York City tomorrow. But delay or not, this year will be the hundredth edition of the parade, and it will still feature celebrities, floats, giant cartoon character balloons and marching bands. The Macy's Great American Marching Band is one of those groups scheduled to perform. NPR's Jennifer Vanasco caught up with them at rehearsal.

JENNIFER VANASCO, BYLINE: High school students are sitting on the grass at an armory just outside New York City, stretched out in the sunshine. Hundreds of them have been at marching band rehearsal all morning, and now they're on a break. They've come from across the country. Some of them are traveling without their parents for the first time...

CHARLOTTE COOPER: I was really nervous at first to meet my roommates.

VANASCO: ...Like Charlotte Cooper from Ellicott City, Maryland.

CHARLOTTE: But all the, like, nerves went away, like, extremely fast 'cause we're all band kids here.

VANASCO: Cooper is a sophomore in high school. She plays the piccolo.

CHARLOTTE: And so we all have a passion for music, and it's just great to be around people who have the same passion as you.

VANASCO: Break is over, and Cooper and her new friends head inside. This afternoon, they're practicing what a national audience will see on TV, which means they have to hit their spot, play their song, and they have 75 seconds to do it.

UNIDENTIFIED INSTRUCTOR #1: Now, so this part should be easier if you bring the right mindset to it.

(SOUNDBITE OF PARTICIPANTS BLOWING RASPBERRIES)

VANASCO: They warm up their mouths and then their instruments.

(SOUNDBITE OF INSTRUMENTS PLAYING)

UNIDENTIFIED INSTRUCTOR #1: Our goal is not to just survive Herald Square, but to actually be able to enjoy it and remember it.

(SOUNDBITE OF MARCHING BAND MUSIC)

VANASCO: Members of the color guard wave their flags and swish their pompoms. The horns shift backwards. The drums move up. They do it over and over...

UNIDENTIFIED INSTRUCTOR #1: Everybody, reset the second.

VANASCO: ...And over. At each pause, staff section leaders rush in and give the students pointers.

UNIDENTIFIED INSTRUCTOR #2: Bass drums, during all of this, can we play twice as loud?

VANASCO: To get into the band, students auditioned by sending in a tape. Once they were accepted, they learned the music on their own, like Cole Lancaster (ph) from Florida. He plays the trumpet.

COLE LANCASTER: Took me, like, two hours 'cause I locked in.

VANASCO: Lancaster says the instructors are pretty strict, but he's learned a lot in a couple of days.

COLE: Just the teamwork and the collaboration to make a really - you know, a great big sound.

VANASCO: By the end of the afternoon, the students are getting tired. They've been standing at attention. Now, they can sit for a moment, but they're still listening to instructions. They're still attentive.

UNIDENTIFIED INSTRUCTOR #1: Now, I know that you've got a pretty good handle on this music, but memorization can always improve.

VANASCO: When they're told to get ready again, they pop up...

UNIDENTIFIED INSTRUCTOR #1: Everybody up.

VANASCO: ...Instruments and flags held high, ready to play. They start to work through a different song.

RICHARD GOOD: (Singing) Jeremiah was a bullfrog.

VANASCO: Band director Richard Good has been with the group since its beginning.

UNIDENTIFIED PARTICIPANTS: Ba-ba, ba-ba, ba, ba...

VANASCO: He says on the long march from the Upper West Side, the students won't just play, they'll sing.

GOOD: (Singing) Jeremiah was a bullfrog.

So that saves their chops on that long parade. So we play that, and then the audience loves it, and then they start singing back.

VANASCO: It's a tremendous experience, he says. Spectators line the streets. They hang out of windows. This is Good's last year. It's his swan song. He's so proud of these students.

GOOD: These guys work so hard. Band is family, and that's truly what it is. If you do it correctly, it's family. You teach them in a short period of time to do what it takes to be done.

VANASCO: But for now, rehearsal is over, except for one last cheer.

UNIDENTIFIED INSTRUCTOR #1: We are...

UNIDENTIFIED PARTICIPANTS: The Macy's Great American Marching Band.

(SOUNDBITE OF MARCHING BAND MUSIC)

VANASCO: Jennifer Vanasco, NPR News, Teaneck, New Jersey.

(SOUNDBITE OF JOHN WILLIAMS AND BOSTON POPS ORCHESTRA'S PERFORMANCE OF "NEW YORK, NEW YORK")

item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

'The Baby-Sitters Club' took tween girls seriously. We're still feeling its impacts

The best-selling book series The Baby-Sitters Club started 40 years ago. NPR member station Connecticut Public has been discussing its legacy with fans for the podcast Generation: Baby-Sitters Club.

JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:

In 1986, a fictional group of eighth-graders in Connecticut started a babysitting business. Kristy, Mary Anne, Claudia and Stacey came from the mind of author Ann M. Martin. "The Baby-Sitters Club" books, hundreds of them, were best sellers. The series celebrates its 40th birthday this year, so our friends at NPR member station Connecticut Public have been talking about its impact with fans and with writers. Connecticut Public podcast host Daniela Doncel is here with us. Hey there.

DANIELA DONCEL, BYLINE: Hi, Juana.

SUMMERS: Hey. So, I mean, first of all, these books were just, like, a huge part of my childhood. But for people who do not remember them maybe as vividly as I do, remind people what "The Baby-Sitters Club" books were all about.

DONCEL: Well, it's really as you said. The books are about a group of tween baby-sitters running a business in Stoneybrook, and readers really identify with the archetypes of these main characters. We have Kristy, who's this lovable tomboy and the president of the club. We have Mary Anne, who is the shy girl shedding her baby image. Claudia is the artist with a huge sweet tooth. And then there's Stacey, the fashionista who lives with diabetes. And the series has grown beyond the books. They've been adapted into two shows, a movie and graphic novels, which are very popular among young readers today. So the club is still going strong 40 years later.

SUMMERS: Oh, yeah. Wow. You're really taking me back here. Now, I know, Daniela, that you went out and talked to a ton of fans about what these books meant to them as they were growing up. What did you hear?

DONCEL: Fans really loved that these characters were so relatable, as well as their entrepreneurship. I think the showrunner of the 2020 Netflix adaptation, Rachel Shukert, who is also a very big fan of the series, she said it best.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

RACHEL SHUKERT: There was something about the way that people just trusted them, that they had these jobs, that they had, like, a place in the world. They had a place in their community. They were known, and they could just kind of, like, do things for themselves. And I loved that.

DONCEL: She emphasized that, really, it was the friendship and it was the independence that stuck with her. And many fans have echoed that.

SUMMERS: I mean, it's been 40 years, which is hard to believe. That is a long time. How do these books hold up?

DONCEL: Yeah. I mean, some things have aged a little bit, right? The girls use a landline phone, which we don't really have those anymore. But the stories certainly hold up. You know, these girls live through chronic illness, academic struggles, relationship troubles, new family dynamics and even grief. Anna (ph) Martin wrote all of this while pulling from her own real life experience as a tween girl.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

ANN M MARTIN: It was just - it was such a hard time, and I wanted the characters to be able to navigate through it. And I was hoping that it would show readers that you can get through that time.

DONCEL: So, really, these books have been able to carry on through generations because of these life experiences.

SUMMERS: When we think about "The Baby-Sitters Club" now, I mean, it's not just a book series. It's so much more. Talk about the legacy.

DONCEL: It's the fact that these books took tween girls seriously before many people were. We learned through the podcast that the term tween really started as a marketing term. Tween girls were being positioned as youthful consumers that might like stereotypically girl things. But then when they became teens, they would quickly be positioned as much more mature consumers. But in real life, tweens were right there in the middle, sometimes growing up feeling embarrassed by what they like. Constance Grady, who was a former Vox critic, voiced this beautifully in the podcast.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

CONSTANCE GRADY: I definitely grew up feeling defensive about how much I liked "The Baby-Sitters Club." I knew that it was something that - it was considered kind of stupid to like. And so I was really worried that people would think that I was stupid for liking it. And that's kind of the way it is with a lot of girl stuff, right?

DONCEL: "The Baby-Sitters Club" books really saw that, and so they humanized tween girls in a way that the consumer market didn't. And we wanted to keep that conversation going with this podcast. Let's take tweenhood and girlhood seriously by talking about it.

SUMMERS: Absolutely. That's Daniela Doncel, a host of "Generation: Baby-Sitters Club." "Generation" is a podcast from Connecticut Public about the media we love and how it shapes us. You can find it at ctpublic.org/generation. Thanks so much.

DONCEL: Thanks, Juana.

(SOUNDBITE OF SEAN ANGUS WATSON'S "WALTZ IN SWEATERS")

A quintessential Route 66 diner has been serving up Americana for nearly 100 years

The Ariston Cafe along Route 66 in Litchfield, Ill., has been a favorite for more than 90 years. Just past the front door, underneath the vintage neon signs that read "Ariston" and "Budweiser," is a diner staple: a glass case, full of sweet temptations. It took one of the Ariston's owners, Will Law, nearly a full minute to reel off all 12 of the day's choices.

"There's a peach crisp bread pudding with the vanilla bourbon sauce," he said. "Then, of course, a traditional cheesecake with or without cherries, and we have a chocolate delight, a lemon delight, a coconut delight."

They were all delightful to look at and the kind of classic American comfort desserts that you might crave while you're road-tripping on America's most famous highway. All of them — like everything else served at the Ariston — are still made in-house.

Litchfield isn't the most natural stop on Route 66; it's a sleepy town about an hour outside St. Louis. But the Ariston Cafe, which sits just across the road from the charming Litchfield Museum & Route 66 Welcome Center, has become an institution in its own right with its wooden chairs and cozy decor.

Travelers still flock to the Ariston, thanks to the internet and social media. The waitstaff says many visitors come in already knowing exactly what they intend to order based on what they've read and seen online.

Right by the front door there's a guest book for diners next to a basket of reading glasses to make reading and signing easier. Within just a few days, the Ariston has welcomed patrons from Australia, South Korea, Nicaragua and Germany, among other nations. And they come from all over the U.S. too.

Bob Dickson celebrated his 75th birthday with his wife, Ann, by traveling Route 66.

"I said to her, 'I would love to go out west to Los Angeles and bring Highway 66 all the way back to where we live,'" he said. "So we did that. We took 31 days, stopped every place you can imagine on and off the highway. We had a great time, an absolutely great time talking to people and just seeing the sights."

On this day's visit, they are just a couple of hours away from their home in Quincy, Ill., and they've stopped for a last celebratory lunch on their big trip. The menu offers so many choices, from patty melts to turkey clubs to pork chops and stuffed shrimp. They said this restaurant, with its throwback vibes and sprawling menu, encapsulates the spirit of their whole road trip.

"It was really adventurous and old fashioned and very joyful," Ann Dickson said.

Opinions run hot about what exactly is the oldest eatery along Route 66, but the Ariston Cafe claims to be the oldest continually operating restaurant on the highway.

Nick Adam is one of the Ariston's former owners. His father, Pete, founded it as a candy shop in 1924. Adam says his father was very young when he arrived in this country.

"He left when he was 10 to come to the United States," Adam explained. "He went back to Greece when he was 12, and then he came back to this country."

Pete Adam seems to have had big ambitions even back then: The shop's name, Ariston, means "the best" in Greek. In 1935, he moved it to its present location on Route 66. Then Nick and his wife, Demi, ran the restaurant for decades.

From first dates to engagements, Demi Adam said the Ariston Cafe has been a fundamental part of this community for decades.

"To be honest," she said, "there's nothing else like this around."

Eight years ago, when the Adams were ready to retire, they sold the restaurant to Will Law and his partners. Law said the Ariston's position as a place locals and visitors alike choose for the big moments in their lives remains unchanged.

"I can't tell you how many wedding proposals have happened in those booths," he said. "We have a couple from Iowa that will come back every year for their anniversary just to have dinner. I see a 50th anniversary at least once a week, if not 60, 65. How cool is that? And they want to share that with you."

In 2006, the Ariston Cafe was put on the National Register of Historic Places. It's another lasting reminder of what this restaurant that steps back in time can mean to visitors in the present.
